source_text: Ac per hoc, si est naturale peccatum tantorum auctor malorum, gratia Christi nequaquam multa delicta donando iustificationem operatur, sed uni peccato indulgendo negotium benignitatis exsequitur; quod cum se spondet acturam, fidem faciet promissis, si haec quae dicuntur per peccati vulnus invecta curaverit; ceterum si et post remedia quae detulit eadem tamen diabolicorum morborum series perseverat, voto eius gratificatio, praesumptioni venia debetur, quia ad curandum innatas pestes virtus ei defuit, non voluntas.
pass_a_gloss: And through this, if there is a natural sin, the author of so many evils, the grace of Christ in no way works justification by giving many offenses, but follows out a business of kindness by indulging one sin; which, when it pledges that it will act, will make faith for the promises, if it shall have cured these things which are said to have been brought in through the wound of sin; but if even after the remedies which it brought the same series nevertheless of diabolical diseases perseveres, gratification is owed to its wish, pardon to its presumption, because toward curing inborn plagues virtue failed it, not will.

lemmas.lexica: LS delictum; Blaise Rom 5 delictum vs donum
LS iustificatio; Blaise forensic making-just, not later system
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: Consequently, if natural sin is the author of so many evils, Christ’s grace certainly does not produce justification by forgiving many offenses. It carries out its work of kindness by pardoning one sin. When it promises to do so, it will make its promises good if it heals the things said to have been introduced through sin’s wound. But if, even after the remedies it has brought, the same succession of diabolical diseases persists, we owe thanks for its good intention and forgiveness for its presumption: it lacked the power to cure the inborn plagues, not the will (compare Romans 5:16).

choices.why: Paul's delictum of the one man; an act, not a nature.
Paul's iustificatio vitae; keep forensic making-just, not a later systematic slogan as default.
